### 📚 Documentation Issue Description

> Related: #116 (first-run installation troubleshooting), #118 (capability entries), #119 (entry-point order). The landing pages and the bucket definitions overlap with #119's navigation ask, so this issue owns their delivery and #119 owns the ordering.

## Summary

PR 122 reorganizes the docs into six buckets per language, but the scaffolding that makes a bucket usable is missing. Five of the six buckets have no landing page, the meaning of each bucket is written only in the PR description, and the user tree has no security page, no general FAQ and no glossary. I would like these standard pages added on top of the structure PR 122 ships.

## Current state

Verified against 0e904661:

- Twelve content directories (six buckets, two languages), and only `developer-docs` has a README in each language. `getting-started`, `core`, `domains`, `how-to` and `reference` have none, so a reader who jumps to a bucket lands on a bare file list.
- What each bucket is for exists only in the PR 122 description. `docs/README.md` names the six buckets in one sentence and defines none of them. Names like `core` and `domains` are not self-explanatory.
- No security or trust page exists in the user tree. The only security text is the multi-user WARNING in `README.md:85-86` (and `README_zh.md:85-86`), which covers loopback binding, the single bearer token, the absence of TLS and the sandbox boundary. The one page that explains isolation, `sandbox-execution.md`, sits in `docs/en/developer-docs/` and `docs/zh/developer-docs/`.
- No general troubleshooting or FAQ page exists. Troubleshooting exists only as per-task sections: the Docker section inside `docs/en/getting-started/deployment.md`, short `## Troubleshooting` sections in `docs/en/how-to/configure-custom-mcp.md:91` and `docs/en/how-to/run-with-jiuwenswarm.md:103`, and a `## 5. Troubleshooting` section in `docs/en/how-to/science-memory-setup.md:187`. The first-run, installation-recovery path is already asked for in #116, which is narrower than a general FAQ.
- No glossary exists. Terms such as Project and Session (used in `docs/en/getting-started/quick-start.md:48`), and Skill, Specialist, Connector, Reviewer and workspace (used across `docs/en/reference/runtime-behavior.md`), have no single definition a new reader can look up.

## What to write

1. Section landing pages. Add a `README.md` to each of the five index-less buckets in both languages, using one template: what this bucket is for, when a reader should come here, and one line for each child page.
2. Bucket definitions. Write the six definitions into `docs/README.md`, so the classification rule lives in the repository and not only in the pull request.
3. Security and trust page. Add a user-facing page in both languages that states the loopback and single-token defaults, the absence of TLS, the fail-closed sandbox and what runs outside it, and the "not a multi-user service" boundary. Link `docs/en/developer-docs/sandbox-execution.md` for depth instead of repeating it.
4. General troubleshooting and FAQ. Add a page in both languages covering model connection failures, permission cards, connector and proxy failures, run timeouts, and where data lives. Keep first-run installation recovery in #116 and link to it.
5. Glossary. Add a page in both languages defining at least Project, Session, Skill, Specialist, Connector, Reviewer and workspace, and link it from the language index.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each of `getting-started`, `core`, `domains`, `how-to` and `reference` has a landing page in both languages, following one template.
- [ ] `docs/README.md` defines what each of the six buckets is for.
- [ ] A security and trust page exists in both user trees and links the sandbox design page.
- [ ] A general troubleshooting or FAQ page exists in both languages and is distinct from the first-run recovery in #116.
- [ ] A glossary page defines at least Project, Session, Skill, Specialist, Connector, Reviewer and workspace.
- [ ] Each new page is linked from its language index, and each landing page links its child pages.

## Open questions

- Should the bucket definitions live in `docs/README.md`, in `CONTRIBUTING.md`, or on a dedicated documentation-style page?
- Does the security page need maintainer sign-off on what is safe to claim before it is published?
- Should the glossary be one page per language, or a section of the documentation home?

## Out of scope

- Page frontmatter and a page status or version schema.
- A machine-readable `llms.txt` or `llms-full.txt` export.
- Changelog or release-notes pages.
- Contributor guides for adding a tool, skill, connector or provider.
- These lower-priority page types are recorded in the audit's deferred list and are not tracked here.

Docs baseline: `feat/jiuwenswarm` @ 0e904661.

issue:137.body:
### 🚀 Background Description


ScienceDiscovery runs Node.js tests in CI but does not yet publish a durable, machine-readable coverage result tied to the exact workflow run and commit. Maintainers should be able to inspect coverage in GitHub Actions, while the status board should consume the same CI evidence without running tests itself or parsing unstable console text.

This issue covers **Node.js coverage only**. Python coverage should be tracked separately so that the tools, test commands, scope, and percentages remain explicit.

The current work-in-progress implementation is PR #134.

### Design Ideas

### Measurement

- Reuse the repository's existing built Node.js tests; do not introduce another test tier or migrate test frameworks.
- Run them with Node.js 22's built-in `--experimental-test-coverage` collector (V8 coverage).
- Group results by workspace/path and keep repository CI-script tests as explicit groups.
- Exclude test sources from production-source totals.
- Record covered/total counts and percentages for lines, branches, and functions rather than storing percentages alone.

### CI execution

- Integrate coverage into the existing `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; do not add a second coverage workflow.
- For pull requests and default-branch pushes, select changed Node.js workspaces and their transitive dependents. Changes to shared coverage infrastructure select every group.
- Reuse the existing nightly workflow for a complete, authoritative all-group baseline.
- Skip coverage for release-only calls.
- Test failures still fail the job. Coverage percentages are informational initially and do not introduce a new threshold gate.

### Actions artifact

- Generate LCOV only as a local intermediate.
- Upload one SHA-qualified artifact containing aggregate and per-group JSON summaries.
- Include source SHA, base SHA, generation time, mode (`incremental` or `full`), selected groups, and whether the result is authoritative.
- Use the repository's default artifact retention; do not introduce independent 30/90-day policies.

### Status-board consumption

- The board downloads the structured summary through the GitHub Actions Artifacts API. It does not execute tests and does not infer coverage from log text.
- Show the latest full nightly baseline, per-path line/branch/function coverage, nightly history, and recent PR affected-group results.
- A homepage value composed from later default-branch group summaries must be labelled as an estimate until the next full nightly run recalibrates it.

### Involved Public APIs

No product runtime or public API changes are proposed.

The feature adds an internal CI artifact contract for coverage summaries. Consumers must treat the run identity, SHA, mode, selected groups, and authoritative flag as part of that contract.

### Description of Relevance to Other Modules

- Existing CI and nightly workflows provide the execution environment.
- Existing Node workspace dependency metadata is used to expand changed workspaces to transitive dependents.
- The companion status board reads the Actions artifact and renders the coverage page.
- Browser/TSX, Python, and Playwright coverage are explicitly excluded from this issue and must not be represented as covered by the Node percentage.
- GitHub Code Quality/Cobertura upload can be evaluated separately; it is not required for the initial board integration.

### Test Design and Test Plan

- Add selector tests for changed workspaces, transitive dependents, shared-infrastructure full selection, and irrelevant-path skips.
- Add aggregation tests that exclude test sources and preserve aggregate and per-group covered/total values.
- Validate that PR/default-branch CI publishes affected-group summaries from the existing CI workflow.
- Validate that nightly publishes a complete authoritative baseline without a second workflow.
- Verify that every artifact is tied to its workflow run/SHA and contains only the structured JSON required by consumers.
- Verify that test failures still fail the coverage job.
- Add status-board tests distinguishing authoritative nightly data, incremental/PR data, estimates, and UT/ST/E2E artifacts.
- Run the repository's complete existing test suite before merging.

### Additional Information

Related work:

- WIP implementation: #134
- Companion status-board PR: https://github.com/ScienceDiscovery/github-status-board/pull/1
- Design in the implementation branch: `docs/designs/test-coverage.v3.md`

Acceptance boundary: the resulting percentage covers built Node.js workspace tests and repository CI-script tests only. It must never be presented as whole-repository coverage.

issue:138.body:
### 🚀 Background Description


ScienceDiscovery contains maintained Python services whose tests are not represented by the Node.js coverage percentage. A Node-only number must not be presented as whole-repository coverage.

This issue adds a separate Python coverage pipeline using mature Python tooling. It complements the Node.js coverage issue #137 while keeping the two languages' commands, reports, and scope independently auditable.

### Design Ideas

### Measurement

- Use `coverage.py` as the coverage engine; do not implement a custom Python tracer.
- Preserve existing test frameworks:
  - `services/gateway` and `services/paper`: `unittest`
  - `services/memory-graph` and `services/evolve`: `pytest`
- Run each existing suite under `coverage run --branch --parallel-mode`, then use `coverage combine`.
- Measure production source directories, not test files.
- Record covered/total counts and percentages for lines and branches. Keep service/path groups separate.

### CI execution

- Reuse existing CI and nightly workflows rather than adding a standalone coverage workflow.
- PR/default-branch runs should select affected Python services where the dependency/selector mapping is reliable. A partial run must be explicitly marked partial and must never be displayed as whole-Python coverage.
- The existing nightly run should execute the complete Python coverage scope and publish the authoritative baseline.
- Coverage remains informational initially; existing test failures still fail the job.

### Reports and artifact

- Generate `coverage.py` JSON as the structured source consumed by the board.
- Optionally generate Cobertura XML for future GitHub Code Quality integration and LCOV/HTML for local diagnosis, without making a paid GitHub feature a prerequisite.
- Upload one SHA-qualified Actions artifact containing aggregate and per-service JSON summaries plus run identity metadata.
- Use repository default artifact retention.

### Dashboard

- Display Node.js and Python coverage as separate first-class metrics.
- If an overall line percentage is shown, compute it from summed covered/total lines:
  `(node covered + python covered) / (node total + python total)`.
- Never average percentages directly.
- Label nightly baselines as authoritative and partial/incremental results explicitly.

### Involved Public APIs

No product runtime or public API changes are proposed.

This feature adds an internal Python coverage artifact contract. It should align with the Node summary's run/SHA/mode/group metadata while retaining Python-specific metrics and source paths.

### Description of Relevance to Other Modules

- `services/gateway` and `services/paper` keep their existing `unittest` commands.
- `services/memory-graph` and `services/evolve` keep their existing `pytest` commands and extras.
- CI test selection and nightly scheduling determine whether the result is partial or authoritative.
- The status board consumes the structured Actions artifact; it does not run Python tests itself.
- GitHub Code Quality can consume Cobertura XML later, but this feature must work without enabling the paid service.

### Test Design and Test Plan

- Add focused coverage runs for every maintained Python service and verify existing tests still execute with the same pass/fail semantics.
- Test combining parallel coverage data from `unittest` and `pytest` environments.
- Verify branch coverage is enabled and test files are excluded from production totals.
- Verify missing/failed service runs cannot produce an authoritative aggregate.
- Verify partial PR results and complete nightly baselines have distinct metadata.
- Validate JSON totals against `coverage report` for representative services.
- Add board parser/rendering tests for Python-only, Node-only, combined, missing, and stale artifacts.
- Verify overall coverage uses summed covered/total values, not the arithmetic mean of percentages.
- Run the complete repository test suite before merging.

### Additional Information

Related work:

- Node.js coverage tracking: #137
- Node.js WIP implementation: #134
- Companion status-board PR: https://github.com/ScienceDiscovery/github-status-board/pull/1
- coverage.py documentation: https://coverage.readthedocs.io/

Non-goals: migrating all Python tests to one framework, implementing a custom coverage engine, or requiring GitHub Code Quality/another paid service.

issue:141.body:
## Summary and current-release boundary

Multi-agent orchestration is a core JiuwenSwarm capability. ScienceDiscovery should explicitly evaluate whether and how to reuse it, rather than silently treating our existing orchestration as the final architecture.

For this release, retain the currently validated hybrid path: **ScienceDiscovery manages delegation through `task`; JiuwenSwarm executes both the main agent and the child agents.** This RFC does not request an immediate migration or block the current release. The eventual reuse decision must be documented with implementation evidence, validation results, and trade-offs.

## Current implementation

The current debugging deployment explicitly selects the platform `task` route. This is a deployment choice, not a claim that every Swarm-backed deployment uses this route.

```text
Main agent (Swarm loop)
  -> ScienceDiscovery task orchestration
  -> Child agent (independent Swarm loop)
  -> Platform task result
  -> Main agent continues
```

ScienceDiscovery currently prepares the specialist profile, enabled MCP/skills, workspace and handoff; manages permissions, concurrency, turn/time limits and cancellation; and records child progress, results and artifacts for the existing UI. The parent receives the result when the `task` call completes.

Swarm's native route uses `subagent_spawn` and `subagent_wait`, with Swarm owning child orchestration. Its integration with ScienceDiscovery-specific bindings has not been fully validated. This does **not** mean Swarm lacks tools, permissions or lifecycle management; the question is how its mechanisms map to the platform's existing behavior.

## Problem and existing evidence

Using Swarm only as the execution engine leaves an important part of its core capability unreused, while switching delegation tools alone risks losing platform behavior. We need a deliberate ownership boundary instead of two overlapping orchestration systems.

A recent real-LLM literature-research run completed through platform `task`: two Swarm-executed children used professional literature MCP tools, returned results, and the parent produced a registered report. This validates that hybrid route only; it does not establish native `subagent_spawn` MCP inheritance, comparative quality, or benchmark-wide reliability.

## Evaluation scope

Evaluate the native route against the current hybrid baseline on the same pinned versions and comparable model/task/tool settings.

| Area | Questions to resolve |
| --- | --- |
| Delegation and scheduling | Who owns creation, concurrency, waiting, completion, and nested delegation? Can we avoid duplicate schedulers and inconsistent state? |
| Context and capabilities | How do specialist instructions, skills, model selection and enabled MCP tools reach each child's actual LLM input? What is inherited versus explicitly handed off? |
| Workspace and science outputs | How do child workspace isolation, sandbox paths, artifact registration, provenance and parent access map to Swarm? |
| Permissions and lifecycle | How are manual approval, automatic approval, cancellation, turn/time limits and partial failures preserved? |
| Results and UI | How are streaming child progress, tool events, usage, errors and final results represented in the existing UI? Does the parent reliably continue? |
| Maintenance | Which extension points already exist? Which minimal upstream fixes/hooks are missing? What platform code could actually be removed? |

Prefer native Swarm capabilities for generic agent behavior. Keep differentiated science functionality in separate modules; intrusive Swarm changes should be limited to bug fixes or necessary extension hooks, not embedding science business logic.

## Candidate outcomes — not a predetermined selection

1. **Native Swarm orchestration plus science extensions:** reuse spawning/waiting/lifecycle and adapt platform capabilities and UI events.
2. **Staged migration:** retain `task` temporarily while closing named native-integration gaps, then transfer ownership with clear exit criteria.
3. **Retain platform orchestration:** acceptable only with concrete evidence explaining why native reuse is unsuitable, its maintenance costs, and conditions for revisiting the decision.

A tool rename or a single successful demo is insufficient to choose between these options.

## Validation and required conclusion

The decision should be backed by deterministic integration tests and a small set of comparable real research runs, not only code inspection.

- Verify actual child LLM tool lists, model routing, skill/context delivery and workspace access.
- Cover parallel children, successful result collection and parent continuation, one child failing, timeout/cancellation, and both approval modes.
- Verify child artifacts remain accessible and traceable, and UI progress reaches a correct terminal state.
- Compare task completion, result quality, token use, elapsed time and resource consumption under comparable conditions; record limitations and failures.

Before closing this RFC, publish a community-reviewed conclusion containing:

- the selected architecture and the rationale for reusing or not reusing native Swarm orchestration;
- a capability/gap matrix with concrete source or test evidence;
- ownership of scheduling, context/tool binding, permissions, lifecycle and science outputs;
- required changes, migration and rollback boundaries, and code that can be removed;
- remaining limitations and follow-up issues, with an explicit distinction between current-release acceptance and the long-term decision.

Related: #84 (Swarm migration), #107 (E2E scenarios).

issue:142.body:
### 🚀 Background Description


The coverage job currently generates and uploads Node.js and Python JSON summary artifacts, but the Actions run page does not expose the results directly. Contributors must download artifacts to see what was scanned and the aggregate coverage, unlike E2E results that are visible in the run summary.

This feature should make coverage results visible without introducing a minimum percentage gate.

### Design Ideas

Write a repository-owned Markdown renderer to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` from the existing `coverage/summary.json` and `coverage/python/summary.json`.

Acceptance criteria:
- Show Node.js and Python separately.
- Label full, incremental, skipped, failed, or unavailable scans.
- Show measured files/groups and available line, branch, and function totals.
- List selected groups for incremental scans.
- Keep coverage informational: no minimum percentage.
- Preserve current failure semantics and artifact uploads.

### Involved Public APIs

None. This changes only GitHub Actions reporting and repository-owned CI scripts.

### Description of Relevance to Other Modules

The change touches `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, the existing Node.js/Python coverage scripts and selector rules, and the operational CI contract in `.ci/README.md`. Runtime APIs and product behavior are unaffected.

### Test Design and Test Plan

- Unit-test the summary renderer for full, incremental, skipped, failed, and unavailable results.
- Test that changes to the renderer select full Node.js and Python coverage.
- Parse the workflow YAML after editing.
- Run the WSL build, recursive workspace tests, and architecture checks.
- Confirm coverage remains informational and coverage test failures still fail the job.

### Additional Information

An implementation is prepared on `wyhohyw:codex/coverage-actions-summary`; a Draft PR will link this issue.

issue:149.body:
## Problem

The `CI` workflow executes the Node and Python unit tests twice.

1. The `UT` job runs `pnpm ci:ut`. That is the gate: with the tagged test plan from #126 it runs the UT slice of the shared plan, selected from source tags and a fixed profile, with every Node test file in a worker of its own and the Python suites through the plan's pytest adapter. The job fails unless every planned case executes and passes. It records no coverage.
2. The `Coverage` job then checks the repository out again and runs `pnpm coverage:node` and `node scripts/run-python-coverage.mjs`, which execute the unit tests a second time under instrumentation. With the plan from #126 they select the very same cases the gate just ran. On a pull request the second run covers only the directories the diff touched; on the nightly schedule it repeats the whole suite.

The second run costs a full test execution per pipeline, and it is a second execution path. The numbers it reports describe a run that is not the one that gated the change. Whenever the two paths differ in how they execute a test — process isolation, interpreter setup, which cases a directory contains — the coverage run passes or fails on its own terms, independently of the gate. Two concrete ways this goes wrong:

- Running a Python service's whole test directory executes cases the gate's profile deliberately leaves out, such as the `status:external` cases in `services/memory-graph` that need a live Neo4j. On a runner without Neo4j those fail the Coverage job while the gate is green.
- Running a directory's Node test files in one shared process lets files interfere with each other's globals. The gate runs each file in its own worker, so cases that pass in the gate can fail under coverage.

## Expected behaviour

- The job that runs the plan records coverage while it runs it. Node workers run with `--experimental-test-coverage` in the same per-file isolation the gate already uses; the Python suites run with `coverage run` in front of the same pytest invocation.
- That job uploads the coverage data as an artifact.
- The `Coverage` job depends on it, downloads the artifact, merges the data and writes the summary. It executes no test. If the producing job failed, the summary is built from whatever was uploaded and states that the job failed; nothing is re-run to fill the gap.
- Pull requests and the nightly run report on exactly the plan the gate ran. There is no separate diff-based selection of what to measure.
- ST and the mocked browser E2E do not load product modules into a measured process, so they contribute no module coverage. The summary says so instead of reporting numbers for them.
- Test selection does not change: source tags and a fixed profile, never the runner's services, credentials or host.

## Acceptance

- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` has no step in the `Coverage` job that runs a test command.
- The coverage files the `Coverage` job reports on come from the gate job's own run.
- A local run of the UT layer produces the same coverage files, and the reporting command runs on them without executing any test.

issue:151.body:
### Background

ScienceDiscovery does not have a recognizable product icon.

The browser tab has a title and no favicon. `apps/web/index.html` has no `rel="icon"` in `<head>`, so the product is indistinguishable from a generic page among bookmarks and tabs.

The in-app brand mark is a generic flask outline (`BrandIcon` in `apps/web/src/icons.tsx`) on an accent square. It fills the slot, but it is not a mark for this product, and it does not read at a 16px tab or bookmark size.

The README opens with a text title and a UI animation. It has no product mark.

### Expected

One product icon, the same mark in all of these places:

1. Browser favicon (at least 16×16 and 32×32, legible on both light and dark tab bars).
2. The in-app brand slot (today’s `.brand-mark`), replacing the generic flask outline.
3. The top of the English and Chinese READMEs, as a product mark. It does not replace the existing UI animation.

The mark has to stay recognizable at small sizes. Do not rely on hairline strokes alone. The drawing, colors, and whether it includes a wordmark are not decided here; this issue does not pre-select a design.

### Out of scope

- The icon is not a control that opens settings.
- The product name and copy stay as they are.
- A desktop or installer icon, if one is needed, belongs with [#34](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/issues/34) (a native desktop window). It does not block the favicon and the in-app mark.

### Acceptance

- [ ] After opening the local web app, the browser tab shows the product icon, not the browser’s default page icon.
- [ ] The sidebar brand slot uses the same mark, not the generic flask outline.
- [ ] The English and Chinese READMEs show the same mark at the top, and the existing UI animation remains.
- [ ] The small icon stays legible on a light UI and on a dark system tab bar.
- [ ] The icon ships in the repository (for example an SVG source plus the small favicon sizes). It does not depend on an external URL.

### Environment

Against current `main` of `openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery`: `apps/web/index.html` has no favicon, and `BrandIcon` is a flask outline.

issue:170.body:
## Motivation

A recent real E2E literature-review run (DRB-59) exposed a reliability gap in the literature-research handoff. The main agent launched six literature-search subagents. Four delivered source artifacts; two spent many tool calls finding sources but failed while attempting to write large Markdown source packages in a single `run_shell` call. Both failed model responses hit the 16,384-output-token limit, their tool arguments were truncated, and no usable artifact was handed back from those two tasks. The parent retried them with smaller writes, but the overall run reached its 60-minute limit before a final report was produced.

The observed failure is in *packaging and handing off the research*, not evidence that the searches themselves were uniformly bad. The current `skills/literature-searcher/SKILL.md` already describes a deduplicated JSON source package, but it does not tell an agent how to checkpoint a long search, bound each write, or resume from partial results. In this run, the delegated instructions instead asked for long Markdown packages with verbatim abstracts, which increased the size of one-shot tool calls.

## Proposed direction for discussion

1. **Make source packages incremental and durable.** Write a small, validated batch of records after each search phase or connector result, then update a compact manifest with counts, query coverage, gaps, and completion status. Keep the downstream JSON contract, or define an explicitly compatible JSONL/manifest handoff. Avoid asking the model to emit an entire large artifact as one shell argument. Preserve DOI/URL, database, citation, and abstract availability without inventing missing metadata.
2. **Keep research content out of the active conversation once saved.** Pass artifact paths plus a concise source index/coverage summary to the parent. Use context compression/checkpoints for long-running research when available, while preserving provenance and the next action. Compression can reduce input-history pressure; it cannot raise the per-response output-token limit that caused these two failures.
3. **Recover cleanly from interrupted writes.** Detect truncated or invalid tool arguments before dispatch, keep already written records, and retry only the unfinished batch at a smaller size. Surface the failure and checkpoint location in the child trajectory so the parent can resume without repeating all searches.
4. **Leave time for synthesis.** The parent should be able to use completed, validated source packages and explicitly report remaining coverage gaps if a retry cannot finish within the run budget. A full retry should not consume the entire report-writing window.

## Questions to settle

- Should the canonical handoff remain one `literature_sources.json`, or should agents append JSONL records and materialize/validate the JSON at the end?
- What is the smallest useful checkpoint (per query, per connector response, or fixed-size record batch), and who owns deduplication across checkpoints?
- Which fields must survive context compression for a parent or replacement subagent to continue the search without losing citation provenance?
- Should the runtime's truncated-tool-argument recovery be tracked here as a dependency or in a separate generic issue?

## Acceptance criteria

- A literature-searcher task with a source package larger than one model response writes valid, deduplicated records progressively and returns a usable handoff without a giant one-shot tool call.
- If a write or model response is interrupted, a retry resumes from the last valid checkpoint and does not duplicate or silently drop sources.
- The parent can consume completed packages, identify missing coverage, and produce a clearly qualified partial report before its deadline.
- An automated test injects an interrupted/truncated write; DRB-59 can serve as a real E2E follow-up, with its report quality assessed separately from this deterministic recovery test.

Related: #141 discusses the two subagent orchestration paths. This issue focuses on the literature-research workflow and artifact handoff, which matter on either path.

issue:175.body:
## Description

When the Nightly workflow runs UT and ST with the `daily` profile, both test jobs produce raw coverage data, but the Coverage job does not receive the corresponding artifacts. As a result, coverage merging fails and the coverage summary is not updated.

Affected run:

- Nightly run: https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/actions/runs/35919083156
- Commit: `9c5a5097336ab5342050dc07f9b14c3ccfce9cd0`
- Actual UT output: `.ci-results/daily-ut/tagged/coverage`
- Actual ST output: `.ci-results/daily-st/tagged/coverage`

The UT and ST jobs themselves completed successfully and wrote coverage data. The failure occurs while handing that data off to the Coverage job.

## Root cause

`test/support/tagged/shared.mjs` includes the profile name in the output label for profiles other than `pr`:

```js
const label = dimensions.length
  ? 'query'
  : profileName === 'pr'
    ? slice
    : `${profileName}-${slice}`;
```

This produces the following paths:

- `pr + ut` → `.ci-results/ut/tagged/coverage`
- `daily + ut` → `.ci-results/daily-ut/tagged/coverage`
- `daily + st` → `.ci-results/daily-st/tagged/coverage`

However, `.github/workflows/ci.yml` still uses profile-independent upload paths:

```yaml
path: .ci-results/ut/tagged/coverage
```

and:

```yaml
path: .ci-results/st/tagged/coverage
```

When Nightly selects the `daily` profile, neither hard-coded path exists. `actions/upload-artifact` therefore reports that no files were found and does not create the `ut-coverage` or `st-coverage` artifact. The Coverage job cannot download those artifacts, merges zero Node.js and Python files, and fails.

This is not a dashboard input-path issue. The data is never uploaded as a workflow artifact, and a later job cannot access the previous job's local workspace directly.

## Regression timeline

- PR #148 introduced the `daily` profile and the `daily-ut` / `daily-st` output naming:
  https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/pull/148
- PR #150 changed Coverage to reuse data produced by the UT/ST jobs, but used hard-coded `ut` / `st` upload paths that do not account for non-`pr` profiles:
  https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/pull/150
- PR #158 enabled hidden-file uploads for the result artifacts, but did not update the coverage artifact paths:
  https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/pull/158

The previous successful Nightly run was:

- https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/actions/runs/35782010015

That run started before PR #150 was merged, so it did not use the current UT/ST coverage-artifact handoff. The `daily-ut` naming introduced by PR #148 is intentional; the regression is the profile-independent artifact path added by PR #150.

## Suggested fix

Avoid hard-coding the `ut` and `st` result directories in the workflow. Possible approaches include:

1. Compute the actual result directory from `${{ inputs.profile || 'pr' }}` and upload coverage from that directory.
2. Have the test runner expose the resolved coverage path as an explicit step output.
3. Use a constrained glob that covers `ut`, `daily-ut`, `st`, and `daily-st` without mixing data from unrelated profiles or slices.

An explicitly computed path is preferable because it avoids accidentally merging data from multiple profiles.

## Acceptance criteria

- The `pr` profile continues to upload and merge UT/ST coverage.
- Nightly with the `daily` profile uploads coverage from `daily-ut` and `daily-st`.
- The Coverage job downloads `ut-coverage` and `st-coverage` and generates non-empty Node.js and Python summaries.
- If UT or ST produces no coverage, the summary identifies the missing layer instead of reporting a misleading zero-file merge.
- The Release workflow continues to skip coverage generation and upload.

issue:185.body:
## Problem

In the `feat/jiuwenswarm` remote Shell Execution flow, the API polls the Runner after the Runner accepts a job. If a status request throws because of a transient communication error, the current implementation can finalize the local record as `unknown / unconfirmed`. This means the remote result has not been confirmed; it does **not** prove that the remote job failed or that the full Agent/skill workflow passed.

## Trigger confirmed from the code

- In `services/api/src/shell-executions.ts`, a `getShellExecution` exception reaches the outer error handler and calls `finish`, turning an accepted execution into `unknown / unconfirmed`. A transient observation error is not sufficiently separated from an authoritative remote terminal state.
- Once the local record is terminal, the normal `execution_status` path does not reconcile that record with the Runner using the original Execution ID. Executions left behind by API restarts or Runner reconnections also need an explicit reconciliation policy.
- The underlying reason for an SSH/Runner status request error still needs investigation. Without a correlated error cause and channel logs, `fetch failed` alone does not establish whether the NPU job, SSH connection, or server failed.

## Suggested reproduction

1. Submit a long-running Shell Execution to a remote Runner and confirm that the Runner accepted it.
2. Make only one **status request** fail transiently while keeping the remote job running.
3. Verify that the API keeps polling the **same Execution ID**, obtains the Runner's authoritative result after connectivity returns, and does not resubmit the command.
4. Also cover consecutive failures, API restart, Runner reconnection, and the complete Agent → skill → NPU artifact flow. See the related end-to-end test in #168.

## Expected fix and acceptance criteria

- Retry recoverable observation errors within a bound, resetting the consecutive-failure count after a successful query. If the result remains unavailable after the threshold, preserve the uncertainty explicitly instead of reporting success or a job failure.
- Provide safe Runner-authoritative reconciliation for `unknown` and restart-orphaned executions without replaying the command.
- Log a correlatable Execution ID, underlying error cause/code, consecutive-failure count, and Runner connection state so an observation-path failure can be distinguished from an actual job failure.
- Cover fault injection in CI without an NPU, and validate the final artifacts through the full Agent/skill workflow in an NPU-enabled environment.

issue:208.body:
Repeated literature connector failures amplify latency across parallel research agents

Real E2E runs on `feat/jiuwenswarm` at `1a0cb9d5` show a non-fatal but significant research-efficiency problem. Agents eventually deliver reports using alternative sources, but continue querying unavailable/rate-limited connectors across independent branches.

## Observations

The experiment ran four cases concurrently, with native task dispatch and Swarm execution, memory graph disabled, and 24 GiB per case. These are observed counts, not a controlled concurrency experiment.

| Run | arXiv failures | Details | Other academic connector failures |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: |
| DRB-62 repeat 1 | 65 | 60 HTTP 406; 5 slot-wait timeouts | 0 Europe PMC/PubMed |
| DRB-62 repeat 2 | 100 | 30 HTTP 406; 46 HTTP 429; 24 slot-wait timeouts | 14 Europe PMC; 6 PubMed |
| DRB-64 repeat 1 | 59 | All arXiv invocations failed | 2 PubMed |
| DRB-64 repeat 2 | 80 | All arXiv invocations failed | 29 Europe PMC; 3 PubMed |

DRB-62 repeat 2 included agent-issued `sleep 30`, `sleep 90`, and `sleep 150` followed by retries. Connector errors included `HTTP 406 Not Acceptable from export.arxiv.org`, `HTTP 429 Unknown Error from export.arxiv.org`, and `arxiv is rate limited and no slot became free within the wait window`. Some upstream failures were surfaced as `retryable:false`, but later calls to the same source still occurred.

Generation time increased from 18.8 to 69.1 minutes for DRB-62 and from 33.2 to 51.2 minutes for DRB-64. This is **not** an attribution of the whole increase to connectors: expanded research scope, synthesis work, and a separate stream disconnect also contributed.

## Investigation / improvement scope

- Diagnose 406 separately from 429: request/endpoint rejection should not be treated as ordinary rate limiting. Verify the actual upstream requests and responses before choosing a fix.
- Make source cooldown/health visible across sibling agents and, where appropriate, concurrent case workers. Confirm existing rate-limit scope before adding another mechanism.
- Honor Retry-After where available; provide bounded admission waits and explicit retry timing. Avoid multiple agents independently sleeping and repeating requests against a persistently failing source.
- Provide actionable fallback guidance without silently changing scholarly evidence requirements.
- Keep low-volume structured diagnostics: source, sanitized endpoint, status, wait duration, retry decision, request/run correlation IDs; never log credentials.

## Reproduction and acceptance

1. Run DRB-62/64 with parallel literature branches and inspect per-source invocation status plus queue waits. The production upstream failure is intermittent, so this alone is not a deterministic reproducer.
2. Add deterministic connector fault injection for sustained 406, repeated 429 with Retry-After, and slot exhaustion across concurrent callers.
3. Verify failures are reported honestly, repeated requests/waits are bounded, cooldown is shared at the intended scope, recovery occurs after cooldown, and alternative sources remain usable.

Local retained evidence (available on the experiment host): `/root/sciencediscovery-real9-3x-20260926/DRB-{62,64}/repeat-{1,2}/data/mcp-invocations/` and `results/artifacts/*/child-trajectories.json`. These paths are not publicly accessible; the aggregate evidence above is included to make the issue independently understandable.

Priority: non-fatal Harness efficiency/reliability follow-up. TC-E2E Judge stability is being fixed separately.

issue:210.body:
## Problem

The local ScienceMemory backend can exhaust memory while building the folded session subgraph. A variable-length `next*0..` traversal enumerates paths across historical sessions before the requested session is filtered, and the interpreter materializes the intermediate rows before deduplication. A small stored graph can consequently require enormous query memory.

This remains reproducible on `feat/jiuwenswarm` at `7a1f0e37`. The relevant `query.py`, `_cypher.py`, and `local_backend.py` files have no diff from the historical incident checkout `d54cfc2d`.

## Historical incident and confidence boundary

During TC-E2E-01 on September 24, 2026:

- The startup log identifies PID 104627 as the memory-graph Python service, listening on port 17876.
- The contemporaneous incident record reports an OOM kill at 04:02:31 Asia/Shanghai, with anonymous RSS of 113,370,408 KiB (approximately 108.1 GiB) for that PID.
- The test stack was interrupted; TC-E2E-01 did not complete, and the next queued DRB-75 case was not started.

The original kernel entry is no longer available in the current journal/dmesg; the RSS figure comes from the retained incident record. There is no Python stack or heap profile from the instant of that OOM. The reproduction below establishes a current, concrete failure mechanism on retained data, but does not prove which exact request was executing at the historical OOM instant.

This is separate from the Node API trajectory/versioning memory problems observed with ScienceMemory disabled.

## Read-only reproduction on retained real graph data

The retained local store contains 4,520 nodes and 5,854 edges. The requested incident session has only **one node**.

Using current code, replay the JSONL records into a standalone in-memory `Graph`, then execute the SQL-like Cypher strings from `get_subgraph` with the incident session ID. Avoid constructing `Graph(Store(...))` directly against original evidence: loading may compact the store. Use a copy or read-only replay.

The diagnostic process was constrained to **512 MiB address space** and a **25-second alarm**. No model calls or service mutations were performed.

| Query | Observed result |
| --- | --- |
| Session nodes | 1 row, approximately 8 ms |
| Direct edges | 0 rows, approximately 18 ms |
| Folded surrogate-edge UNION | `MemoryError` after approximately 3.95 seconds, peak RSS approximately 502 MiB |
| Same folded query, with an early `WITH scope, first WHERE scope.session_id = $sid` before each variable-length match | 0 rows, approximately 1 ms |

The failure stack is inside `_match` / `_match_parts`. Early filtering is a diagnostic control, **not a complete fix**: querying an affected, branched session can still enumerate a huge number of paths.

## Mechanism

1. [`get_subgraph`](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/7a1f0e37/services/memory-graph/src/sciencediscovery_memory_graph/query.py#L164) builds folded surrogate edges using:

   ```cypher
   MATCH (scope:Task)-[:contains]->(first:ToolCall)
   OPTIONAL MATCH (first)-[:next*0..]->(child:ToolCall)
   MATCH (child)-[:produces]->(c:Code)-[:produces]->(art:Artifact)
   WHERE scope.session_id = $sid
   ...
   RETURN DISTINCT ...
   ```

   The same traversal shape occurs in other UNION branches. The local interpreter does not push the later session predicate before the preceding variable-length match.

2. [`_walk`](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/7a1f0e37/services/memory-graph/src/sciencediscovery_memory_graph/_cypher.py#L1290) tracks used relationships per path. It enumerates relationship-simple paths rather than unique reachable endpoints. A DAG can therefore cause combinatorial growth without any cycle.

3. [`_match`](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/7a1f0e37/services/memory-graph/src/sciencediscovery_memory_graph/_cypher.py#L1171) appends all matching rows to a list. Projection, DISTINCT, and output LIMIT happen later, so small final output does not bound intermediate memory.

4. The retained `next` graph has 1,677 vertices and is acyclic, but contains **41 branching nodes**: 33 mix `scope_chain` and `temporal_chain` edges, four have multiple `scope_chain` edges, and four have multiple `temporal_chain` edges. This traversal does not filter by `method`. Dynamic programming on this DAG counts **237,316,988 paths, including zero-length paths, from one scope entry**.

5. [`LocalSession`](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/7a1f0e37/services/memory-graph/src/sciencediscovery_memory_graph/local_backend.py#L48) uses a shared graph store across sessions and holds a graph-wide lock for the transaction. Historical data can affect a new nearly-empty session, and an expensive query can block other graph operations.

The origin of the extra chain branches is **not yet established**. Inspect chain rebuilding and scope/temporal edge membership rather than assuming a particular write race.

## Suggested fix scope

- Filter session/scope before traversal and prevent crossing unrelated scopes or chain types.
- For folded reachability views, compute the required reachable products/`via_child` identities without enumerating every path. Do not globally replace Cypher path semantics where callers actually require distinct paths.
- Investigate and validate chain construction/rebuild invariants; cover mixed chain types and historical stores.
- Add bounded intermediate-work/memory handling and cancellation so a graph query cannot take down the scientific task stack. Output limits alone are insufficient.
- Preserve low-volume query diagnostics: query identity, duration, graph size, traversal/intermediate counts, termination reason. Do not log sensitive graph contents by default.

## Acceptance / regression coverage

- A new nearly-empty session remains cheap to query when unrelated historical sessions contain branching chains.
- A deterministic small synthetic DAG with repeated branch/rejoin structure completes a folded reachability query with bounded work, correct deduplication, and preserved `via_child` information.
- Querying an affected session itself is safe; early session filtering alone is not considered sufficient.
- Cycles, mixed scope/temporal chains, rollback, and existing subgraph behavior retain their intended semantics.
- Validation runs under a strict process memory/time cap, avoiding another host OOM.

## Retained evidence

Local experiment-host paths (not publicly accessible):

- `/root/sciencediscovery-pr171-e2e-run/status.json` and `stack.log`
- `/root/.science-agent/memory-graph/{nodes,edges}.jsonl`
- `/root/sciencediscovery-memory-graph-diagnosis/{findings.md,probe.py,original-query.log,early-filter.log}`

The counts, query shape, guarded reproduction results, and uncertainty boundaries are included above so this issue is understandable without access to those private experiment files.

# 中文版

## 版本定位

ScienceDiscovery **全面拥抱 jiuwen-swarm 后端的第一个 Beta 版本**：保留科研工作台体验，以 jiuwen-swarm 支撑 Agent 执行，在新架构上整合科研专属能力。

本 issue 用于征集社区对 Release Note、发布范围及阻塞问题的反馈，**不是正式发布公告**。上一版本为 `0.2.0`；建议版本号为 **`0.3.0-beta.1`（待确认）**，开发主线为 `main`（原 JiuwenSwarm 分支已切换为主线），本次发版分支为 `releases/v0.3.0.beta`。

## Release Note 草案

### 重点支持场景

本版本重点保障以下四类场景，不追求一次性迁移全部历史能力或覆盖所有边界情况。

| 场景 | 主要流程与交付 | Domain 文档 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 文献调研 | 检索与获取文献、提取证据、多专家协作，交付带可追溯引用的调研报告 | [文献调研教程](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/releases/v0.3.0.beta/docs/zh/domains/literature-research.md) |
| 数据分析 | 读取数据、准备环境、执行分析，交付可复现代码、图表与结论 | [脓毒症数据分析教程](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/releases/v0.3.0.beta/docs/zh/domains/analyze-sepsis-endotypes.md) |
| 抗体设计 | 结合领域 Skill、专业模型和科研环境完成设计与筛选；依赖相应模型资源与算力，计算结果不等同于实验验证 | [抗体设计教程](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/releases/v0.3.0.beta/docs/zh/domains/antibody-design.md) |
| 算法优化 | 通过科研产物 RSI / Evolve 生成候选、执行评估与迭代，保留结果与过程记录 | [算法优化教程](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/releases/v0.3.0.beta/docs/zh/domains/evolve-a-solution.md) |

### 核心功能与改进

- **统一 JiuwenSwarm 默认后端**：源码、Docker 和发行包启动器均默认选择 JiuwenSwarm；保留显式 native 切换。主子 Agent 默认通过平台 `task` 委派、由 Swarm 执行，并非全面切换为 Swarm 原生多 Agent 编排。
- **科研执行环境与工作区**：支持本地/远程执行、托管环境、后台任务、文件传递、工作区交接及产物版本关联。
- **记忆图谱**：记录科研任务、文件与产物关系，支持引用追溯；源码及 Docker 部署提供默认本地存储，可选 Neo4j。
- **科研 Skill、MCP 与 Specialist**：支持内置能力和自定义扩展，组合专业专家完成科研任务。
- **科研产物 RSI 与 Idea Tree**：支持产物迭代优化、候选评估和研究思路的树状探索。
- **可观测性与测试**：完善执行轨迹、子任务状态和错误诊断，补充 Mock E2E、真实科研 Benchmark 与质量评估记录。
- **文档与入门体验**：整理中英文文档和四类场景教程，明确 Swarm/native 在上下文、规划、工具、Skill 等方面的行为差异。

这些功能包含已有能力的迁移与增强，并非全部首次引入。

### 官网、社区与交付配套（本版本新增）

- **统一对外网站**：提供[官网与安装入口](https://sciencediscovery.github.io/install/index.html)，集中展示安装指引、使用文档与科研场景教程；网站内容随 `main` 分支同步更新。
- **用户交流社区**：面向海外与中国用户，分别建立 **Slack** 和 **飞书**用户交流群，用于使用交流、问题反馈与社区协作；加入方式见仓库首页。
- **双分支每日 CI**：构建每日质量检查，覆盖 `main` 和 `releases/v0.3.0.beta`。由 main 的定时任务触发两条分支各自的检查，分别保留结果、日志和构建产物，为主线演进与版本发布提供持续质量反馈。
- **多平台、多种安装方式**：支持 Linux、macOS，Windows 可通过 WSL 2 使用；提供源码、Linux 二进制发行包及 Docker 等部署方式。不同系统可用的安装方式与前置条件不同，详见[官网安装页](https://sciencediscovery.github.io/install/index.html)。

### 主要 Bugfix

- **记忆图谱内存与查询性能**：修复折叠查询的路径爆炸，使用共享路径及累计集合预算，避免已复现的高内存分配；超预算返回结构化错误。优化会话索引查询，避免大量无关历史数据拖累新会话（#212，修复 #210）。
- **启动行为一致性**：修复源码与 Docker/发行包默认后端不一致，确保命令行后端选项优先于 `.env`；Docker 转发 Swarm 配置，E2E 显式选择后端（#214）。
- **Swarm/MCP 隔离与恢复**：改进模型、会话、工具绑定隔离，工具刷新、共享连接和权限生命周期（#173、#181、#182）。
- **子任务与远程执行可靠性**：改进并发排队、超时、取消、工作区交接和子 Agent 恢复；远程执行状态查询增加瞬时错误重试（#182、#187、#191）。
- **模型输出与事件流**：改进截断输出恢复，避免执行不完整工具参数，增强工具事件流存活与诊断（#190、#194）。
- **科研数据与交付**：改进 PDF 校验、arXiv 接入兼容性、产物版本关联，以及界面状态、快照作用域和取消诊断（#171、#180、#192、#179、#189、#193）。

## Beta 边界与升级说明

- **Nightly Real E2E 尚不稳定**：自动真实模型 E2E CI 仍在稳定化过程中，当前真实科研场景的验收以本地实际执行并保留记录的结果为准，需注明被测提交、模型和配置。Nightly 结果作为辅助诊断，不单独作为版本质量已达标的依据；跳过或隔离的用例不视为通过。UT/ST/Mock E2E 门禁仍是独立的质量依据。
- **部分安装路径为实验特性**：macOS Docker 以及所有 Windows 安装路径（包括 WSL 2 和 Docker Desktop）尚未全面验证 Agent 执行效果。当前预编译单文件包面向 Linux，不提供原生 macOS/Windows 二进制；macOS 优先使用源码方式，Windows 的 Linux 二进制/源码方式需在 WSL 2 内运行。具体支持范围与依赖见官网安装页。
- **官网与发行版的差异**：官网跟随 main，可能包含尚未进入本次 Beta 的更新；本版本的准确行为与限制以发行分支文档和最终 Release Note 为准。
- **场景验收与效果边界**：四类场景是重点验收范围，效果仍受模型、网络、数据源和算力影响；测试已加入不代表所有真实场景已稳定通过，发布以最终候选版本验收为准。
- **Swarm 初始化与后端切换**：源码首次使用 Swarm 前执行 `scripts/jiuwenswarm.sh setup`。保留原生循环可使用 `--no-jiuwenswarm` 或 `SCIENCE_AGENT_EXECUTOR=native`。
- **记忆图谱升级与故障处理**：升级不会覆盖已保存的记忆功能设置；此前手动关闭的用户需在系统设置中重新开启。已有图谱可通过 `SCIENCE_AGENT_MEMORY_GRAPH_DATA_DIR` 指向原目录，不自动迁移。设置 `SCIENCE_AGENT_MEMORY_GRAPH_AVAILABLE=0` 可跳过服务；该可选服务启动失败时会报告原因并在禁用图谱的情况下继续启动，修正后需重启。
- **外部数据源限制**：arXiv 406/429、排队超时等外部数据源问题仍由 #208 跟踪。

## 社区反馈

请反馈：版本定位与版本号是否合适、功能或修复有无遗漏、四类场景是否存在发布阻塞，以及哪些限制必须写入正式说明。问题反馈请附配置、复现步骤及日志。

# English version

## Release positioning

This is ScienceDiscovery’s **first Beta release embracing the jiuwen-swarm backend**. It retains the scientific workbench experience, uses jiuwen-swarm for Agent execution, and integrates science-specific capabilities into the new architecture.

This issue collects community feedback on the release notes, scope, and blockers; **it is not a release announcement**. The previous version is `0.2.0`. The proposed version is **`0.3.0-beta.1` (to be confirmed)**, with development on `main` (the former JiuwenSwarm branch) and this release prepared from `releases/v0.3.0.beta`.

## Draft release notes

### Priority scenarios

This Beta focuses on four scientific workflows rather than migrating every historical capability or covering every corner case.

| Scenario | Workflow and deliverables | Domain documentation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Literature review | Search and retrieve literature, extract evidence, collaborate across specialists, and deliver a report with traceable citations | [Literature research tutorial](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/releases/v0.3.0.beta/docs/en/domains/literature-research.md) |
| Data analysis | Inspect data, prepare an environment, execute analysis, and deliver reproducible code, figures, and conclusions | [Sepsis data analysis tutorial](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/releases/v0.3.0.beta/docs/en/domains/analyze-sepsis-endotypes.md) |
| Antibody design | Combine domain Skills, specialized models, and scientific environments for design and screening; requires appropriate model resources and compute, and computational results do not constitute experimental validation | [Antibody design tutorial](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/releases/v0.3.0.beta/docs/en/domains/antibody-design.md) |
| Algorithm optimization | Generate, evaluate, and iterate on candidates through scientific-artifact RSI / Evolve, retaining results and execution records | [Evolve a solution tutorial](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/releases/v0.3.0.beta/docs/en/domains/evolve-a-solution.md) |

### Core capabilities and improvements

- **Consistent JiuwenSwarm default**: source, Docker, and packaged launchers now select JiuwenSwarm by default, with an explicit native opt-out. Subagents default to platform `task` delegation with Swarm execution—not a complete switch to Swarm-native multi-agent orchestration.
- **Scientific environments and workspaces**: local/remote execution, managed environments, background tasks, file transfers, workspace handoffs, and artifact-version associations.
- **Memory graph**: research-task, file, and artifact relationships with traceable citations; source and Docker deployments provide local storage by default, with optional Neo4j.
- **Scientific Skills, MCP, and Specialists**: built-in capabilities and custom extensions for domain-expert collaboration.
- **Scientific-artifact RSI and Idea Tree**: iterative artifact optimization, candidate evaluation, and tree-based exploration of research ideas.
- **Observability and testing**: improved trajectories, subtask status, and diagnostics, alongside Mock E2E, real scientific benchmarks, and quality-evaluation records.
- **Documentation and onboarding**: reorganized English/Chinese documentation and tutorials for the four workflows, with explicit Swarm/native differences in context, planning, tools, and Skills.

These include migrations and enhancements of existing capabilities, not exclusively new features.

### Website, community, and delivery infrastructure (new in this release)

- **Unified public website**: the [website and installation hub](https://sciencediscovery.github.io/install/index.html) bring together installation guidance, documentation, and scientific workflow tutorials. Website content is kept in sync with `main`.
- **User communities**: **Slack** and **Feishu** groups have been established for international and China-based users respectively, supporting usage discussions, feedback, and community collaboration. See the repository homepage for joining instructions.
- **Daily CI for both branches**: daily quality checks cover `main` and `releases/v0.3.0.beta`. The scheduled main workflow triggers independent runs for both branches, retaining separate results, logs, and build artifacts to support development and release validation.
- **Multiple platforms and installation options**: Linux and macOS are supported, with Windows access through WSL 2. Options include source installation, Linux binary packages, and Docker. Availability and prerequisites vary by platform; see the [installation hub](https://sciencediscovery.github.io/install/index.html).

### Major fixes

- **Memory-graph query performance and memory use**: eliminate path explosion in folded queries, introduce shared paths and cumulative collection budgets for reproduced allocation failures, and return structured budget errors. Indexed session queries avoid scanning unrelated historical data (#212, fixes #210).
- **Consistent startup behavior**: align source defaults with Docker/packages, make CLI backend selection override `.env`, forward Swarm settings through Docker, and select E2E backends explicitly (#214).
- **Swarm/MCP isolation and recovery**: improve model/session/tool binding isolation, tool refresh, shared connections, and permission lifecycle (#173, #181, #182).
- **Subtask and remote-execution reliability**: improve admission queues, timeouts, cancellation, workspace handoffs, and subagent resumption; retry transient remote execution-status failures (#182, #187, #191).
- **Model output and event streams**: recover from output truncation without executing incomplete tool arguments, and improve tool-stream liveness and diagnostics (#190, #194).
- **Scientific data and delivery**: improve PDF validation, arXiv compatibility, artifact-version associations, UI state, snapshot scope, and cancellation diagnostics (#171, #180, #192, #179, #189, #193).

## Beta limitations and upgrade notes

- **Nightly Real E2E is not yet stable**: automated real-model E2E CI is still being stabilized. For now, acceptance of real scientific workflows relies on recorded local runs, identifying the tested commit, model, and configuration. Nightly results provide supplementary diagnostics, not standalone proof of release readiness. Skipped or quarantined cases are not passes; UT/ST/Mock E2E gates remain independent quality evidence.
- **Some installation paths are experimental**: macOS Docker and all Windows paths (including WSL 2 and Docker Desktop) have not been fully validated for Agent execution. Current prepackaged single-file binaries target Linux, not native macOS or Windows. Prefer source installation on macOS; Linux binaries/source installation on Windows run inside WSL 2. Consult the installation hub for platform-specific requirements and support boundaries.
- **Website versus release documentation**: the website follows main and may describe updates not yet included in this Beta. Use the release-branch documentation and final release notes for the exact behavior and limitations of this version.
- **Workflow acceptance and outcome limitations**: The four workflows are priority acceptance targets. Outcomes depend on the model, network, data sources, and compute. Having tests does not establish that all real scenarios pass reliably; release acceptance must use the final candidate.
- **Swarm setup and backend selection**: Before first using Swarm from source, run `scripts/jiuwenswarm.sh setup`. Use `--no-jiuwenswarm` or `SCIENCE_AGENT_EXECUTOR=native` to retain the native loop.
- **Memory-graph upgrades and failure handling**: Upgrades preserve saved memory preferences; users who previously disabled memory must re-enable it in System Settings. Use `SCIENCE_AGENT_MEMORY_GRAPH_DATA_DIR` to retain an existing graph directory; data is not migrated automatically. Set `SCIENCE_AGENT_MEMORY_GRAPH_AVAILABLE=0` to skip the service. If this optional service fails to start, the launcher reports the cause and continues with memory disabled; correct the cause and restart.
- **External data-source limitations**: External-source failures, including arXiv 406/429 responses and queue timeouts, remain tracked in #208.

## Community feedback

Please comment on release positioning/versioning, missing features or fixes, blockers in the four workflows, and limitations that must appear in the final notes. Include configuration, reproduction steps, and logs for reported problems.

## Problem

Successful real research runs still have a large per-case memory footprint for individual users. On current `feat/jiuwenswarm`, the highest observed worker cgroup peak is **11.12 GiB**. Although the latest GraphMemory fix prevented the previously observed runaway behavior in this experiment, this steady operational footprint deserves separate investigation and reduction for ordinary personal computers.

This is a resource-efficiency issue, not a report of another GraphMemory OOM. It is separate from #210 / its fix #212.

## Measured evidence

Experiment revision: `17d0774a` (includes #212 and TC Judge fix #209).

- Nine real scientific E2E cases, three repetitions each; four case workers concurrently.
- GraphMemory enabled throughout, local backend, isolated graph directory per case/repetition.
- Native task dispatch with Swarm execution; generator/Judge `deepseek-flash`.
- Each worker has a 24 GiB cgroup limit and no swap. The group includes the platform stack, graph service, Swarm, Runner and descendants, browser, and Judge.
- All 27 attempts delivered successfully. Retained `memory.events` show `max=0`, `oom=0`, `oom_kill=0` for every worker.

| Case / repetition | Worker cgroup peak (GiB) | Sampled Node API RSS peak (GiB) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| TC-E2E-01 / 1 | 11.124 | 0.977 |
| DRB-75 / 1 | 11.123 | 1.127 |
| DRB-62 / 2 | 10.796 | 0.952 |
| DRB-75 / 3 | 10.397 | 1.275 |
| DRB-59 / 2 | 10.107 | 1.080 |

The three worker peaks for TC-E2E-01 were 11.12 / 8.27 / 8.43 GiB; DRB-75 was 11.12 / 8.61 / 10.40 GiB. Even PUCT's workers peaked around 4.41 GiB in this setup.

**Measurement boundaries:**

- Cgroup peak includes charged file cache and other memory, not just anonymous RSS. It is not proof that the application requires 11 GiB of unreclaimable working memory.
- API RSS is sampled separately and its maximum need not coincide with the group peak. Do not subtract these maxima to infer another component's usage.
- GraphMemory did not appear in the retained high-RSS process samples, but these contain only the host's top 12 processes above a threshold, so its precise individual peak cannot be recovered.
- This harness includes Playwright and diagnostic sampling. Startup/provisioning, browser, diagnostics, page cache, child agents, and runtime costs must be separated before attributing the footprint to the product or GraphMemory.
- Concurrent cases and agent choices varied; this is not a controlled concurrency-scaling measurement.

## Why this matters

Users on 8–16 GiB machines also need memory for the OS, browser, and other applications. Raising per-worker limits or recommending large-memory hosts is not an adequate resource-efficiency strategy. We need to establish the actual working set and provide a practical personal-machine configuration without silently dropping research evidence or quality requirements.

## Investigation and optimization plan

1. Record `memory.stat` (`anon`, `file`, `kernel`, `slab`, etc.), `memory.current/peak/events`, and memory pressure alongside process-tree attribution for the **specific worker cgroup**. Capture phase markers for startup, provisioning, child research, synthesis, and grading.
2. Sample process RSS/PSS by role: API, Swarm/gateway, graph, Runner/executions, browser, Judge. Keep diagnostics lightweight and credential-free; measure profiler overhead explicitly.
3. Reproduce TC-E2E-01 and DRB-75 alone and with concurrent child tasks. Measure the idle stack separately and compare with/without the browser/profiling overhead. Preserve GraphMemory and the same delivery/scoring contract.
4. Identify avoidable duplication or retention only from profiles: repeated runtime processes, scientific environments/imports, per-agent contexts, trajectory buffers, graph state, caches, and teardown. Do not assume any one is the culprit from aggregate peaks.
5. Optimize the dominant confirmed contributors. If required, provide explicit resource-aware concurrency/backpressure and document the latency tradeoff rather than changing research tasks or silently disabling capabilities.

## Acceptance criteria

- Produce a component/phase memory breakdown for the highest-footprint cases, distinguishing reclaimable cache from working memory.
- Establish a measured baseline and a concrete lower memory budget suitable for a representative personal machine, with headroom for OS and interactive use; do not invent a target before attribution.
- Demonstrate improvement against that baseline on the same tasks, with GraphMemory enabled, no OOM, retained artifact delivery, and quality scoring reported independently.
- Check memory release after task completion and repeated use within a long-lived session; include lightweight regression monitoring where practical.

Retained evidence on the experiment host (not publicly accessible):
`/root/sciencediscovery-real9-graph-3x-20260927/case-summary.csv`, plus each case's `memory.csv`, `memory-events.txt`, and `memory-profiles/memory-*.jsonl`.

issue:22.body:
## Goal

Make ScienceDiscovery a useful, approachable research product. A researcher should be able to understand what it can help with, get started with clear guidance, complete a task, and return to their work confidently.

The first experience we should deliver is simple:

**Open the app → connect a model → upload a CSV and ask a question → receive a useful chart → refine and save the result.**

The application should handle routine setup and organization, ask only for decisions that matter, and explain the next step in plain language. Technical details should be available when needed.

## Why this matters

During a trial of release 0.2.0, a new user encountered welcome cards that did not navigate, confusing model setup, unexplained `Unauthorized` messages, and an interface that opened even though analysis could not run on that computer. These problems prevented the user from experiencing the product's value.

This evidence comes from one installation. Check fixes in the current release and development branch before opening duplicate work. Related public feedback includes [difficulty finding the download](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/issues/1).

## Improvements

### 1. Make the starting point obvious

- Explain the product with one concrete example and show its finished result.
- Provide prominent **Get started**, **Try an example**, and **Watch the walkthrough** actions.
- Make every suggested action work. Clearly explain unavailable actions and how to enable them.
- Offer a visible English/中文 switch and consistent wording throughout the experience.

### 2. Guide the user through setup

- Provide one recommended download and setup path for each supported computer type.
- Ask for the minimum information needed to connect a model, with helpful defaults and a clear connection test. Explain any required API key, where to obtain it, and that provider usage may incur charges.
- Handle the app's internal connection automatically where possible. If a user must reconnect, take them directly to a guided recovery step.
- Check that analysis can actually run before showing the app as ready. Explain compatibility problems early and provide a concrete next action.
- Keep advanced configuration accessible outside the ordinary setup flow.

### 3. Make everyday work feel straightforward

- Let users start with a question or a file. Create the initial project/session automatically for the guided example.
- Show understandable progress based on what is happening, such as reading data or preparing a chart. Make waiting, required input, completion, and failure easy to distinguish.
- Provide visible stop/retry actions where appropriate. Preserve the user's question and files when something fails.
- Explain errors in plain language with a recovery action; place diagnostic details behind an expandable option.
- Present the result clearly, with an explanation, supporting evidence, and access to the producing code. Make follow-up requests, saving/exporting, and returning later easy to discover.

### 4. Provide two videos that help people understand the product

**Video 1 — From opening the app to a first result (5–7 minutes).** Show a real released version: download/open, connect a model, upload the supplied CSV, ask a question, inspect the chart, request a change, and reopen the saved work. Provide the sample file, prompt, transcript, and English/Chinese captions. Show required preparation and label accelerated waits.

**Video 2 — The same task with and without ScienceDiscovery (6–8 minutes).** Use IMO 2026 Day 2 Problem 5 to compare the same model in direct conversation and in ScienceDiscovery. Focus on the viewer's experience: what they ask, how much guidance they provide, how understandable and complete the answer is, and how easily they can inspect or continue the work. Also report actual time and cost.

Keep the problem, model, and budgets comparable; review the mathematical proofs and report the observed outcome, including ties or failures. The problem's answer is the family `f(x) = x + c`, with `c >= 0`; describe it as the complete solution family. See the [original problem](https://www.imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2026/2026_eng.pdf) and [published reference proof](https://github.com/AxiomMath/IMO2026/blob/main/IMO2026/Q5/solution.lean).

Both videos must reflect working released behavior. Their purpose is to explain the experience and demonstrate useful outcomes. Test the app's guidance with new users, including people who have not watched the videos, and fix the points where they get stuck.

### 5. Make feedback and contribution welcoming

- Provide an obvious way to ask for help or report a problem without requiring users to understand the architecture.
- Explain where contributions are reviewed and how GitHub visitors reach that destination. The [current contribution guide](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/907382ce42e1ebfe77e24281905dec0607aaf003/CONTRIBUTING.md) routes code contributions to GitCode.
- Offer a short first-contribution guide and a few bounded tasks with named reviewers. Useful examples include improving a confusing screen, contributing an analysis example, or fixing a connector.
- Document checks newcomers can run without paid model access or special hardware, and how maintainers help with the remaining validation.

## How we know this is better

- [ ] A new user can explain what ScienceDiscovery does and identify how to start.
- [ ] On a supported computer, the user can complete the sample analysis, refine the result, and reopen the saved work without live maintainer assistance.
- [ ] Setup problems are explained before the user starts dependent work; failures preserve their inputs and offer a clear next step.
- [ ] The main journey works in English and Chinese, and the displayed controls and instructions match the released app.
- [ ] Both videos are linked from the project entry page, use actual runs, and include the materials needed to follow or inspect them.
- [ ] A new contributor can find a suitable task, run the relevant checks, submit a change, and understand the review process.

Observe ten unfamiliar users and use eight completing the sample journey without intervention as an initial target. Also record where users get stuck, whether they return the following week, and whether contributors return for another contribution. These are proposed targets, not current results.

## Delivery

Prioritize the first-use journey and recovery from the problems already observed. Validate the downloadable release, record the videos, and improve the experience with a small pilot group before broader promotion. Give each follow-up a named owner.

# English version

## Positioning

ScienceDiscovery now has a [public website](https://sciencediscovery.github.io/) where visitors can learn about the research workspace, explore the home-page demo, and continue to the [installation page](https://sciencediscovery.github.io/install/index.html) and [documentation](https://sciencediscovery.github.io/docs/index.html). This issue expands on the website work mentioned in the [#213 Beta release-note draft](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/issues/213).

This is a request for community feedback on the website's content, navigation, and onboarding experience. It is not a formal software release announcement, and the demo does not establish that every depicted workflow has passed live validation.

## Draft website launch notes

### Home page: understand and explore

- **Product overview and entry points**: the home page introduces the ScienceDiscovery research workflow, a quick Linux installation path, core capabilities, and links to installation and documentation.
- **An interactive demo that starts on its own**: the HTML demo presents a workbench-like interface. When it comes into view, a scripted literature-review workflow plays once. Visitors can follow the task, tool calls, and artifacts without taking any action, much like watching a short video.
- **Hands-on exploration**: visitors can choose another scripted scenario, replay it, click nodes, switch views, and adjust chart or structure controls. The scenarios illustrate literature research, Idea Tree, Evolve, the memory graph, and scientific data visualizations.

The demo uses scripted flows and illustrative data to show product capabilities. It does not run a live research task against the product backend, and its charts and structures are not experimental results.

### Installation page: choose a path for your environment

The [installation page](https://sciencediscovery.github.io/install/index.html) organizes options by Linux, macOS, and Windows and explains the prerequisites and steps for prebuilt Linux binaries, Docker, and source mode. It provides release downloads and SHA256 checksums, post-start checks, and links to the full deployment guide. Some platform paths are marked experimental. Consult the page for current prerequisites.

### Documentation: go deeper

The [documentation](https://sciencediscovery.github.io/docs/index.html) offers English and Chinese entry points, navigation, and full-text site search. Readers can explore getting started, core capabilities, domain guides, advanced setup, reference material, and developer documentation. The website builds these pages from the [ScienceDiscovery repository's `docs/` directory](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/tree/main/docs). Documentation content is maintained upstream. The website provides its presentation and navigation.

## Version relationship and usage notes

The website documentation follows the product repository's `main` branch and may describe changes that are not part of a particular release. Download links on the installation page can also change as the site is updated. Check the [installation page](https://sciencediscovery.github.io/install/index.html) and [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/releases) for the versions available when you visit. For the behavior and limitations of a specific release, use its release notes and version-specific documentation.

## Community feedback

We welcome feedback on whether the home-page demo communicates the product clearly, which interactions or descriptions could be misleading, how easy it is to find an installation path and its prerequisites, and any gaps in documentation navigation, search, or English and Chinese content. For a page issue, please include its URL, browser, and steps to reproduce.
